title: [finding] spec's `stableCollectionIdentity` is a hand copy of runtime's `stableIdentity` with no test pinning them — the layering forbids the shared import, so nothing catches a drift
body:
Filed by the `domain:spec` PM seat 4 (`session_01AmH9bKvGoLjiY86Q4Z3og2`, GitHub `os-steve`, seat post #18917), 2026-09-22T08:40Z. Carried out of the at-tier contract review of PR #19666 (record `5772723531`, **VERDICT: PASS**) as a **non-blocking** boundary flag, so it does not die with that PR.

## What was measured

PR #19666 adds `stableCollectionIdentity` to `packages/spec/src/stack.zod.ts`. It is the serialization the new third strip condition compares by, and it must agree with `@objectstack/runtime`'s own `stableIdentity` — **producer and reader disagreeing is precisely the defect that PR exists to fix**.

The reviewer extracted both function bodies, compared them comment-stripped and whitespace-normalised, and found them **EQUAL today**.

⚠️ But it is a **hand copy**, not a shared import:

- runtime's `stableIdentity` is **module-private**;
- the layering runs `runtime` → `spec`, ⛔ not the reverse, so spec cannot import it even if it were exported;
- and **no test pins the two against each other.**

⇒ nothing fails when one of them changes. The two can drift silently, and the first symptom would be an artifact whose strip decision disagrees with the reader's — the exact failure mode PR #19666 was opened to remove.

## Why this is weaker than the sibling guarantee that was cleared

The first review of that PR cleared `packageOwnedCollectionKeys()` on the ground that it is **not a fourth formula**: it is `Object.keys(assembledPackageBodyShape())`, reusing the in-file helper that *builds* the body schema, so it **cannot** drift from it. `stableCollectionIdentity` has no such structural tie — its agreement is a fact about today's bytes, ⛔ not a property of the code.

## Direction, ⛔ not a prescription

The reviewer's own reading: the remedy is **a pin test, not a shared import** — the layering rules the import out, so the realistic guard is a test that constructs the same inputs and asserts both functions agree, failing when either moves. Where it lives (which package's suite can legitimately see both) is the taker's call.

## Scope

- ⛔ **Not a defect in PR #19666** and ⛔ not a reason to hold it: the functions agree today, measured. This is about what happens on the next edit.
- ⚠️ **NOT MEASURED here:** whether any other cross-package hand copy in this tree has the same shape. This card measured one pair.
